idiom_name: @Entity/@Table/@Column annotations read by the JPA provider
implementation_notes: Metadata lives in annotations on the entity: @Entity, @Table(name = "users"), @Id with @GeneratedValue, @Column(name = "user_name"), @Transient, with @Access deciding whether fields or getters are the mapping source. The reader is the provider's metadata layer (Hibernate's annotation metadata reader), which builds a persistent metamodel - tables, columns, types, associations - when the SessionFactory starts, and the engine is EntityManager plus the provider's JDBC layer performing CRUD and queries from that metamodel, so no per-class mapper is written. Field access is the usual default; when the classes must stay annotation-free, the identical metamodel can be built from XML mapping files instead.
pitfalls: Field versus property access is decided by where @Id sits; mixing annotations on fields and getters in one class splits the mapping in ways the provider only warns about.
Lazy loading through proxies means equals/hashCode and detached graphs behave unlike the metadata suggests, and a mapping tweak can silently change fetch behaviour.
Annotation defaults (naming strategy, column length, nullability) differ between provider versions, so an upgrade can change the effective mapping of unmapped columns.

variants.name: External mapping files (orm.xml / hbm.xml)
variants.implementation_notes: The mapping is declared outside the code in an XML document - Jakarta's META-INF/orm.xml or the older Hibernate hbm.xml: an entity element naming the class and table, then id and basic element/column pairs. The provider's XML metadata reader builds the same persistent metamodel, so the engine is unchanged; what changes is that domain classes carry no persistence annotations and the mapping can be replaced or split per deployment, which is the historical form the pattern was described with. Choose it when different products persist the same classes differently or when missing annotations must not be visible in the code; it is a poor fit for teams that want the mapping next to the field.
pitfalls: Two mapping sources: when annotations and XML both exist, XML wins for the elements it declares, so the effective mapping is split across files and tools disagree about what they see.
XML mapping errors surface when the persistence unit starts or at deployment, often far from the changed document, and the compiler never sees them.
